beats.lead: Most people who've used OKRs at work credit Google for them.
beats.text: Google adopted the system. It didn't invent it.
beats.note: By the time OKRs reached Google, the method had already been running inside another company for decades.

beats.name: Andy Grove
beats.role: Built the system inside Intel and called it 'iMBOs' — Intel Management by Objectives — drawing on Peter Drucker's older idea of managing by objectives from the 1950s.

beats.lead: One of Grove's own students carried it out the door.
beats.text: John Doerr joined Intel in 1974 as a salesman and sat in Grove's internal course in 1975, where he first learned the iMBOs method.
beats.note: He later wrote the book that gave it its modern name: 'Measure What Matters.'

beats.context: How long the method had already been running at Intel before Doerr, by then a venture capitalist, introduced it to Google's founders in 1999.

beats.lead: Grove wasn't impressed by where Doerr took it next.
beats.text: When Doerr left Intel for the venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins in 1980, Grove told him venture capital 'is not a real job. It's like being a real estate agent.'
beats.note: Grove wrote the method down just once, in his 1983 book 'High Output Management.'

beats.line: A 1970s Intel habit, still wearing the name Google made famous.
